_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 6 specification: one article, six gaps, SEVEN sentences A–G, one of them extra. Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (it, a real bus, them, the whole scheme, what nobody had predicted, the same thing) and forwards to the next sentence (she had no good answer, children waiting at a stop, Claire's response, the solution, teachers reported, neighbours). The extra sentence (F) tempts gap 5, which is about the road outside the school, but 'as long as ever' contradicts 'and it got it', and it gives the teachers' reports about the children nothing to follow. Used by the Part 6 practice page.
title: All aboard the walking bus
subtitle: One mother left her car at home for a single morning. Five years later, half a town walks to school.
text: Every morning at half past eight, the narrow road outside St Aldric's Primary School in Fenwick Green used to turn into a car park. Parents queued, reversed and argued over spaces, a few hundred metres from the gate. Claire Hollis, a mother of two who lived barely ten minutes' walk away, was as guilty as anyone. {1} She had no good answer. So, one Monday in September, she left the car at home and set off on foot with her two sons and, as it turned out, three of the neighbours' children.

Word spread quickly. Within a fortnight other parents wanted their children to join, and Claire realised she needed a system. She drew a route through the estate, with five 'stops' at street corners and a timetable showing when the group would pass each one. {2} Children waiting at a stop simply joined the line as it went by, and a parent at the back made sure nobody was left behind.

The 'walking bus', as the children named it, ran smoothly until November. Then the weather turned, and so did some of the parents. {3} Claire's response was to buy a box of cheap waterproof ponchos so bright that one father compared the children to a flock of ducklings. They loved them, and on the wettest mornings the bus was, if anything, fuller than usual.

A bigger problem was finding adults. Each route needed at least two volunteers every morning, and most parents had jobs to get to. {4} The solution came from an unexpected direction. A notice in the newsagent's window attracted four retired residents, among them a former lollipop man, who were happy to walk a mile in return for, as one of them put it, 'a reason to get dressed before ten'.

By the following spring there were three routes and nearly sixty children. The school had expected one benefit, a calmer road at the gate, and it got it. {5} Teachers reported that pupils who arrived on foot were more settled in the first lesson, and far less likely to be late.

There were other surprises, too. Children from different streets, who had barely spoken before, became friends on the way to school, and several shy pupils found they had plenty to say once they were walking side by side. {6} Neighbours who had never spoken began stopping to chat at the 'bus stops', and one elderly volunteer was invited to so many birthday parties that she began saying no.

Five years on, the walking bus still leaves the corner of Orchard Lane at eight o'clock every morning. Claire no longer runs it; that job belongs to the former lollipop man, who takes it very seriously. The road outside the school is quiet. And Claire's car, she admits, spends most of the week on the drive, collecting leaves.
sentences: What nobody had predicted was the effect on the children themselves.
For several weeks the whole scheme depended on Claire and two other mothers, who were beginning to look exhausted.
Like a real bus, it would leave each stop at exactly the same time every day, whether anyone was waiting or not.
The same thing, rather to their surprise, began to happen among the adults.
Faced with heavy rain and dark mornings, several of them announced that their children would arrive soaked, and quietly went back to driving.
Even so, the queue of cars outside the gate was as long as ever.
It was her six-year-old son who finally asked why they drove to a school he could see from his bedroom window.
why: 'It was her… son who finally asked' follows Claire being 'as guilty as anyone'; his question leads to 'She had no good answer'.
'It' is the group on its route with stops and a timetable; 'each stop' leads to 'Children waiting at a stop simply joined the line'.
'Them' is the parents who 'turned' with the weather; the fear that children would 'arrive soaked' is answered by 'Claire's response' of waterproof ponchos.
'The whole scheme depended on Claire and two other mothers' shows the shortage of adults; their exhaustion is the problem that 'The solution' then solves.

'What nobody had predicted' contrasts with the benefit the school 'had expected'; 'the children themselves' leads to what teachers reported about pupils. F is tempting because it is about the road, but 'as long as ever' contradicts 'and it got it'.
'The same thing' is making friends, and 'among the adults' contrasts with the children; the neighbours chatting at the bus stops then give examples.
